strengths: The paper performs a systematic, well-motivated bottom-up ablation of optimizer components (normalization types and momentum placement), which is a useful contribution to the growing but fragmented literature on memory-efficient optimizers.

Clear empirical findings: column-wise normalization is shown to be nearly as effective as more expensive singular-value normalization at a fraction of the compute cost (Table 1, Table 2), and last-layer momentum is empirically and theoretically motivated via layer-wise gradient variance analysis (Figure 3).
A convergence theorem (Theorem 2.1) for layer-wise momentum SGD is provided, offering some theoretical grounding for the intuition that momentum benefits layers with higher gradient variance most.

Extensive experiments spanning model sizes from 60M to 7B parameters, including comparisons against a wide range of strong baselines (Adam, Stable-SPAM, Muon, GaLore, Fira, APOLLO(-Mini), SWAN), with careful memory accounting in the appendix.

The resulting algorithm (SCALE) is simple to implement, requires minimal code changes over Adam, and achieves competitive perplexity with substantially reduced memory footprint (35-45% of Adam), making it a practically useful minimalist baseline.
Good discussion connecting the proposed method to prior works (SWAN, Scion, Muon) and clarifying differences (e.g., not applying Adam to first/last layers unlike SWAN).
weaknesses: The core algorithmic ingredients (column-wise/steepest-descent normalization framework, last/first-layer special treatment) are largely drawn from or closely related to existing work (Bernstein & Newhouse 2024, Pethick et al. 2025 Scion, SWAN, Muon); the contribution is primarily a careful combination and ablation rather than a fundamentally new technique, which somewhat limits originality.

The theoretical analysis (Theorem 2.1) is derived for plain SGD with per-layer momentum but explicitly *without* column-wise normalization, whereas the actual proposed algorithm (SCALE) combines both. The paper acknowledges it cannot extend the analysis to explain the joint benefit of normalization and momentum together, leaving a gap between theory and the final method.

At the 1B scale, SCALE does not clearly outperform Stable-SPAM (13.97 vs 14.25) or Muon (14.18 vs 14.25) in perplexity, and the 7B result relies on a single non-repeated run without a full learning-rate sweep, which limits confidence in the claim that SCALE 'matches or exceeds' fully adaptive optimizers at scale.

Several baseline numbers (Adam, Stable-SPAM, GaLore, Fira, SWAN, APOLLO on 7B) are copied from other papers rather than reproduced under identical experimental conditions, which may introduce inconsistencies in hyperparameter tuning effort or hardware/precision settings across comparisons.

Training uses a relatively short sequence length (256) and single-seed runs for most experiments, and no variance/error bars are reported, making it hard to assess statistical robustness of the (often small) perplexity gaps between methods.
Limited ablation on sensitivity of the last-layer momentum coefficient β beyond a single default (0.9), despite this being a key hyperparameter of the proposed method.

strengths: Systematic, well-motivated bottom-up ablation study that isolates the contribution of gradient normalization schemes (singular-value, column-wise, row-wise, sign) and momentum placement, providing genuine insight into which Adam components matter most for LLM pretraining.

Extensive empirical validation across model scales (60M to 7B parameters), including a rare 7B pretraining comparison against Muon and APOLLO, where SCALE achieves both better perplexity and lower memory.

Broad set of supporting experiments beyond the main pretraining results: throughput benchmarking, additional architectures (Qwen2, GPT2, Gemma), overtraining regime, fine-tuning on GLUE, and learning-rate sensitivity, which substantially strengthens claims of generality.

A convergence analysis (Theorem 2.1) that connects layer-wise gradient variance to the benefit of momentum, providing a plausible theoretical rationale consistent with the empirical variance observations in Figure 4.

Careful and transparent memory accounting (Appendix A.1) making the memory-performance trade-off claims verifiable and the method easy to reproduce, requiring only minor code changes to a standard Adam implementation.

Insightful diagnostic analysis (Figure 3, Figure 7, Appendix A.9) explaining mechanistically why row-wise normalization destabilizes the LM head due to token-frequency-driven gradient imbalance, adding interpretability to the design choice.
weaknesses: Theorem 2.1 explicitly excludes column-wise normalization from the analysis ('we did not consider column-wise normalization for ease of theoretical analysis'), so the theory only justifies the momentum component and not the full combined method that is actually deployed; the paper itself even declines to give a full convergence proof for Algorithm 1.

The theoretical result shows that convergence is monotonically improved by higher β for every layer (optimal is βl = 1-δ for all l), so the decision to apply momentum only to the last layer is justified mainly by the informal argument that other layers have σl ≈ 0, which is supported only by a single qualitative variance plot (Figure 4) rather than rigorous quantification across layers/models.

Some reported results are inconsistent with the paper's headline claim of 'matching or exceeding' Adam: e.g., for the 1B model, Adam (Stable-SPAM) achieves 13.30 perplexity vs. SCALE's 13.49 (Table 5), meaning SCALE is actually outperformed by the strongest Adam baseline in that setting.

Most experiments (including the important 7B run) appear to be single runs without multiple seeds or reported variance, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of the (often modest) perplexity differences between SCALE and competitive baselines like Muon and Stable-SPAM.

The core novelty is somewhat incremental: column-wise normalization is already used in Scion/SWAN, and applying different treatment to the last/first layers is a well-established idea in GaLore, Fira, APOLLO, and SWAN; SCALE's distinguishing choice (momentum-only, no second moment, applied solely to the last layer) is a relatively small variation on this existing design space.

SWAN results are copied directly from the original paper due to code unavailability rather than being reproduced under the authors' own experimental pipeline, which weakens the fairness of some memory/perplexity comparisons.

For the 1B experiments, Fira and APOLLO required reduced learning rates due to divergence with their default settings, raising a question of whether all baselines received comparably thorough hyperparameter tuning at that scale, given the paper notes wandb sweeps were only performed up to 350M and manual tuning was used beyond that.
